text: NIST SP 800-61 groups Containment, Eradication, and Recovery under one phase name, but they're three separate jobs done in sequence, not one action with three labels. Containment stops the bleeding — it limits an attacker's ability to do further damage or spread further, right now, before anything else happens.

Eradication removes the actual cause — the malware, the unauthorized account, the vulnerability that let the attacker in — so the problem doesn't simply resume once things calm down. Recovery returns affected systems to normal operation, verified clean, and brings the business back to running as usual. This lesson is only a high-level overview; Chapter 4 covers Containment and Eradication in real depth, and Chapter 5 does the same for Recovery.

The order matters because each phase depends on the one before it actually being finished. Attempting Eradication before Containment means trying to remove malware from a system an attacker can still actively reach and reinfect — a losing battle. Attempting Recovery before Eradication means restoring a system to 'normal' while the actual cause is still present, which just invites the same incident again, often within hours.

Take the compromised-workstation example from Lesson 1, now with these three phases filled in properly. Containment disconnects the workstation from the network, cutting off its ability to reach a command-and-control server or spread to other machines. Eradication identifies and removes the actual malware that caused the outbound traffic, confirming it's gone rather than merely quiet. Recovery restores the workstation from a known-clean image, verifies it's behaving normally, reconnects it, and confirms with monitoring that the unusual traffic doesn't return.

Only after all three are complete does the incident move into Post-Incident Activity from Lesson 1, the lessons-learned review that feeds back into Preparation. Each phase has real depth a single overview can't cover responsibly, which is exactly what Chapters 4 and 5 are for. Up next, Chapter 2 goes deep on what a real incident response plan actually contains, picking up right where Lesson 2 left off.
